For certain molecules or molecular ions, two or more equivalent Lewis diagrams can be written. An example is ozone (O3), for which there are two possible Lewis diagrams:

These diagrams suggest that one OUO bond is a single bond and the other one is a double bond, so the molecule would be asymmetric. In fact, the two OUO bond lengths are found experimentally to be identical, with a bond length of 1.28 Å, which is intermediate between the OUO single bond length in H2O2 (1.49 Å) and the OuO double bond length in O2 (1.21 Å).

The Lewis model fails to predict the correct structural formula for O3. The Lewis model handles such cases by saying that the actual bonding in O3 is repre- sented as a resonance hybrid of the two Lewis diagrams in each of which one of the bonds is intermediate between a single bond and a double bond. This hybrid is represented by connecting the diagrams with a double-headed arrow:
O O O
O O O

The term resonance does not mean that the molecule physically oscillates back and forth from one of these bonding structures to the other. Rather, within the limita- tions of the Lewis dot model of bonding, the best representation of the actual bond- ing is a hybrid diagram that includes features of each of the acceptable individual diagrams. This concept of resonance arises because the Lewis model very strictly defines a chemical bond as a pair of electrons localized between two nuclei. In cases like O3 where the electrons are delocalized over the entire molecule, we seek an- other bonding model to overcome this limitation in the Lewis model. The need for resonance is avoided by using molecular orbital theory to describe chemical bond- ing (see Chapter 6).
